newsitem.title: USA: McVeigh admits planting Oklahoma City bomb - newspaper.
newsitem.headline: McVeigh admits planting Oklahoma City bomb - newspaper.

text.p: Oklahoma City bombing suspect Timothy McVeigh admitted planting the bomb that killed 168 people and told his defence team he launched the attack during the daytime to kill a high number of people, The Dallas Morning News reported on Friday.

The newspaper said in a special report published on its Internet page that it had obtained confidential defence team documents summarizing several interviews with McVeigh in which he detailed preparations for the April 19, 1995, attack which killed 168 people.

It said McVeigh implicated his co-defendant Terry Nichols in the bomb plot but insisted that he alone drove the explosives-filled truck that destroyed the Alfred P.Murrah federal building in downtown Oklahoma City.
The newspaper said McVeigh's lead attorney Stephen Jones would not confirm the contents of the documents but said they were either stolen or fake and should not be published.
"I don't presume to know everything everybody has said ... but none of that sounds familiar to me," The Dallas Morning News quoted Jones as saying.

But the newspaper said it obtained the documents legally and that one of them detailed a 1995 interview in which McVeigh explained why he did not explode the bomb at night, when the federal building would have been empty.

"Mr. McVeigh looked directly into my eyes and told me 'That would not have gotten the point across to the government. We needed a body count to make our point'," the defence team staff member wrote in notes of the interview, according to the newspaper.

The newspaper said McVeigh told his defence interviewers the bomb was built with 5,400 pounds (2,400 kg) of ammonium nitrate fertiliser and $3,000 worth of high-powered racing fuel. If true, the bomb was even bigger than police had thought.

McVeigh, who is to go on trial in a Denver court on April 1, has pleaded not guilty to the bombing charges but The Dallas Morning News said he did not deny the attack in any of the documents it had examined.

The documents were based on meetings with McVeigh between July and December 1995 at El Reno Federal Correctional Institution in Oklahoma, where he was held before being transferred to the Denver area in March 1996.
Because the documents detail interviews with defence team members, prosecutors will not have access to them and they will probably never be introduced to the jury, the newspaper said.
It said McVeigh also detailed two 1994 robberies which he planned and Nichols carried out in order to bankroll the bombing.
